title: Right mindfulness
hookLine: the four foundations, now as a factor of the path (MN 141)

cards: In the Deer Park near Benares, where he first taught, the Buddha gives his monks a brief summary of the four noble truths.

Then he praises Sariputta and Moggallana, says Sariputta can explain the truths in detail, gets up, and goes into his dwelling. It's one of the moments the canon records him handing the teaching to a student.
Sariputta takes it from there, truth by truth, factor by factor, and when he reaches the seventh factor of the path, he defines it in one long, careful sentence.

teach.b: Sammā sati. Sati is usually translated mindfulness, but it corresponds to the Sanskrit smṛti, memory.
So mindfulness here is less like a spotlight and more like remembering: remembering to notice, remembering what you're doing while you're doing it. Sariputta's sentence runs like this.
A practitioner dwells contemplating the body as body, ardent, clearly knowing and mindful, having set aside wanting and grief about the world. Then feelings as feelings. The mind as mind.
And dhammas, the patterns of experience, as dhammas. Four foundations; the first year spent three weeks on them. What's new is where they sit.
On their own, they're a meditation method.

teach.h: A WORKING PART OF THE PATH.
teach.b: As the seventh factor of the path, they're a working part of something larger.
Right view tells mindfulness what to look for. Right effort supplies the energy to keep looking.
Right concentration, later on the path, gathers what mindfulness has noticed into stillness.
And in the great forty sutta, where three factors circle around each of the others, mindfulness is one of the three: it's there inside right speech, right action, right livelihood, all of it.

That's why the line is so plain. Not a special state you visit on a cushion, but a habit of remembering, in an ordinary day, that you're here, in a body, feeling something, thinking something, and that you can see it.

how: Buddhists practice right mindfulness through satipaṭṭhāna meditation, often beginning with the breath, and through attention carried into daily activity; in Theravada the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta is widely chanted and studied.

o: a trance that empties the mind of thought
a calm feeling that comes from deep rest

s: sati corresponds to a Sanskrit word for memory
smṛti: mindfulness is remembering to notice.
in MN 141 the Buddha himself gives the detailed explanation
he gives a summary, then Sariputta explains it in detail.
right mindfulness works alone, apart from the other factors
MN 117 has it circling every factor, with right view and right effort.

games.q: you're a monk in the Deer Park. the Buddha has summarized the four truths and praised Sariputta and Moggallana. what happens next?
o: he goes into his dwelling, and Sariputta explains it in detail.
he asks the monks to debate it.
games.why: in MN 141 the Buddha rises and enters his dwelling, and Sariputta analyzes the four truths, including each factor of the path.

practice: Touch all four foundations, about half a minute each: the body where it meets the seat; whether this moment feels pleasant, unpleasant or neither; the mind, calm or restless, sleepy or bright; and whatever pattern is here, a wanting, a pushing away, some ease.
Each time you drift, remembering is the practice, and if you have five minutes afterward, stay.

wordCard.voice: Sammā sati. Right mindfulness: the four foundations, body, feelings, mind and dhammas, as the seventh factor of the path.

orig.note: Pali sammā sati: right mindfulness, the seventh factor of the eightfold path; sati corresponds to Sanskrit smṛti, memory.

carryVoice: Your line: remember to notice. Mindfulness is a habit of remembering, not a place you visit. See you tomorrow.
